source.title: Bad Students Make Great Teachers: Active Learning Accelerates Large-Scale Visual Understanding
source.authors: Talfan Evans; Shreya Pathak; Hamza Merzic; J. Schwarz; Ryutaro Tanno; Olivier J. Hénaff

page_placements.theme: Data quality, relevance and selection change scaling efficiency

record.file_problem: No apparent truncation or garbling; the full paper text, including supplementary material, is present.
record.tranche_reason: The study runs compute-scaling experiments and reports whether scaling behavior carries over to active data selection, using image models and held-out accuracy rather than language-model loss.
record.gate_note: The paper cites language-model scaling laws and reports its own visual-model compute-scaling results in Figure 5. The JFT results use held-out top-1 accuracy, not held-out cross-entropy loss, and do not fit or report power-law exponents. Other active-learning and transfer results do not test the listed scaling-law versions. Downstream transfer scores are not reported as a predictability relationship with scale or pretraining loss.
record.test_reason: Scaling laws serve as motivation and frame. The study reports how much compute its own data-selection methods (ClassAct, ActiveCLIP) save over uniform sampling. Figure 5 plots JFT top-1 accuracy, not loss, against FLOPs for a ViT-L with and without active selection. It fits no power law, reports no exponents and gives no readable values. The authors' sentence that their results 'generalize' scaling laws to non-uniform sampling is an assertion; no fit backs it. The uniform ViT-L curve reproduces Zhai et al.'s setup and is used only as a baseline. Figure 5 therefore measures the method's savings over that baseline, not whether a power-law form holds.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right. The authors conclude that learnability scoring with small proxy models is the first active-learning method to save total FLOPs at large scale. They report 46% and 51% fewer updates and up to 25% less total compute on JFT and ALIGN. They say the method shifts uniform-sampling scaling laws in its favour. They speculate, without testing, that more aggressive selection might yield better-than-power-law scaling.
record.recipe_differences: The study uses visual ViT pretraining with active data selection and held-out classification accuracy, rather than language models and held-out cross-entropy loss; it does not fit the original power-law relationships.
record.method_sensitivity: The compute savings differ between learner-only and total-compute accounting; the text says ViT-S produces larger, marginal learner savings than ViT-Ti, while the difference is less pronounced for total FLOPs.

fits_no_version.finding: Learnability-based active data selection with small actors (ViT-Ti, ViT-S) shifts the ViT-L JFT accuracy-vs-compute curve left. Savings at matched accuracy are about 25–33% across the compute budgets tested, and the total-FLOP savings remain after counting scoring cost.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Model-based data selection can shift scaling curves, reducing the compute needed for a given performance relative to uniform sampling.

record.problems: The scaling experiment uses visual classification accuracy rather than held-out loss, and the paper reports no fitted exponents or explicit power-law fit for Figure 5. The relevant curves are figure-only in the supplied text, with no uncertainty estimates stated.
record.rows_left_out: No rows omitted. Figure 5 is the only reported compute-scaling sweep directly relevant to V5; other active-learning results do not test the listed scaling-law versions.

untested.parts: Whether vision-model loss, or loss under non-uniform data selection, follows a power law in compute. No fit or exponent is reported; the uniform ViT-L curve is only a baseline.
Extrapolation from small runs to larger runs.
Compute-optimal allocation of parameters and tokens.
Effect of model shape at fixed parameter count.
Predictability of downstream performance from scale or pretraining loss.
Dependence of fitted exponents on setup and fitting choices.

record.verdict_notes: The reader's 'tests/T2' with V5 'supports' is overturned. Figure 5 has no fit, uses accuracy rather than loss, and compares the study's own method against a baseline. The authors' words 'scaling laws for active learning' are framing, not a test of the power-law form.

versions.untested_parts: Held-out language-model pretraining loss versus parameter count, tokens, or compute.
Extrapolation from smaller language-model runs to much larger runs.
Compute-optimal parameter and token allocations for language models.
Effects of architecture shape at fixed parameter count on language-model loss.

The study tests visual classification under active data selection, but does not fit a power-law form or exponents; it does not test video, repeated data, fine-tuning, or transfer as scaling-law regimes.
Predictability of downstream task performance from scale or pretraining loss.
Dependence of fitted exponents or compute-optimal allocation on counting, schedule, data, or fitting choices, and bending of curves away from a power law.
